newsitem.title: USA: Corn, wheat prices drop sharply, coffee also weak.
newsitem.headline: Corn, wheat prices drop sharply, coffee also weak.

text.p: Grain prices fell on Tuesday as corn planting in the Midwest continued at a rapid pace and better weather in the Plains states helped the winter wheat crop battered by a freeze three weeks ago.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn for May delivery closed 4-1/2 cents a bushel lower at $2.88-1/2.
The Agriculture Department said 50 percent of the nation's corn crop was planted as of Sunday, compared to just 18 percent a week earlier and 40 percent a year ago.
"If you get the crop planted early, history tells us that you should get big yields," said Doug Hjort, president of consultants Hjort and Associates in Adel, Iowa.
That message was not lost on speculators, who sold heavily after betting earlier that cold weather and flooding might cut corn supplies this year.
Speculators also bailed out of the wheat market as supply concerns eased. Wheat for May delivery closed 11-1/4 cents a bushel lower at $3.94, its first close under $4 in a month.
European wheat fields received badly needed rains, breaking drought fears in Spain and France.
Weekly crop reports from Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas issued on Monday also showed that damage from the April 12-13 freeze may not have been as drastic as first thought.

Most crop scouts on a tour of central Kansas wheat fields sponsored by the Wheat Quality Council on Tuesday forecast yields equal to or above those of last year in areas with generally low incidence of disease. But they had yet to tour southern Kansas areas where the freeze hit hardest.
Winter wheat harvest has already started in southern Texas, with leaf rust disease cited as a problem.

Soybean prices were under pressure from rapid planting progress in the Midwest, but a rumor about Brazil restraining its booming soybean exports caused May soybeans to close one cent a bushel higher at $8.94.

"There was talk Brazil might reinstitute some kind of export tax," said Bob Lekberg, an analyst with Goldenberg-Hehmeyer. "This is the same talk that floated around a few weeks ago. In the final wash, I think it won't go through."

Spokesmen for Brazil's Agriculture and Finance Ministries said the country had no plans to tax soybean or soyproduct exports. Domestic Brazilian soybean processors had not renewed their request for a tax put forth a few months ago, they said.
At the New York Cotton Exchange, cotton for May delivery set a new life-of-contract low for a second straight day and closed at 70.20 cents a pound, down 0.08 cent.

"It may be that the market is trying to tell us that world consumption is not increasing as fast as we thought it would," said O.A. Cleveland, a marketing specialist with Mississippi State University. "Given the reasonably strong world economy, there may be more competition from the polyester."
As of Sunday, only 25 percent of the cotton crop had been planted compared to 31 percent last year.
"Rain in the Delta should provide some support, but the market seems to be ignoring it," said Judith Ganes, a Merrill Lynch analyst.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee prices took a breather after pushing near three-year highs.

Coffee for May delivery closed at 249.60 cents a pound, down 1.30 cents. The day's high of 254.00 cents came within 10 cents of the 263.50 cent level reached in July 1994, when a frost badly damaged the crop in Brazil, the world's top coffee producer.
News that Colombia's truck drivers threatened to launch another nationwide strike did little to ward off sellers.
"It's a correction," said Refco analyst Ann Prendergast.

Coffee warehouse stocks remain extremely tight. After the close of trading on Tuesday, the exchange said warehouse coffee stocks certified for delivery against futures dropped a sharp 13,999 bags to 27,699 bags as of May 5. Each bag contains 132 pounds of coffee.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, heating oil prices rose as traders expected to see a drawdown in stockpiles in weekly statistics from the American Petroleum Institute to be issued after the close of trading.

Heating oil for May delivery closed 0.48 cent a gallon higher at 53.53 cents a gallon. June crude oil ended 3 cents a barrel higher at $19.66 and June unleaded gasoline closed down 0.23 cent a gallon at 60.31 cents.
